tree.title: Root
tree.task: Write a research brief on how one person can run a reliable multi-agent coding workstation that survives losing their laptop: backup, cloud workstations, agent coordination, cost control.
tree.rationale: The brief spans four distinct areas (data durability, hosted compute, multi-agent orchestration, spend control), and each needs its own research into current tools. They can be researched in parallel if the boundaries are drawn so that all money questions go to one subtask and all questions about recovering the environment go to another.

children.title: Backup and laptop-loss recovery
children.task: Research how one developer running AI coding agents can lose their laptop and be working again within hours. Cover: what has to survive (git repos including unpushed branches and worktrees, dotfiles, agent configuration such as CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, skills, MCP server configs, hooks, settings, session transcripts or memory files, and local databases); how to handle secrets and credentials (password managers, secret stores, re-issuing tokens, MFA recovery codes) without putting them in backups as plain text; backup tools and patterns (git remotes, dotfile managers such as chezmoi, restic/borg/Backblaze or cloud sync, full-disk images versus declarative rebuilds such as Nix, devcontainers or bootstrap scripts); and restore drills with target recovery times. Leave out choosing or comparing cloud workstation providers and any cost analysis. Deliverable: a brief section (about 800-1200 words) with a recommended baseline setup, a checklist of items to back up, a step-by-step restore procedure for a new machine, and a list of trade-offs and limitations, citing sources for any tool behavior you claim.
children.rationale: The deliverable is one 800-1200 word section on a single coherent topic. Its parts depend on each other: what to back up shapes the tools, and the tools shape the restore steps. Splitting it would mean merging overlapping research on the same tools (git, chezmoi, restic, password managers), which adds overhead without improving coverage.
children.result: This node checks the official docs for the tools it names and writes one brief section. Sources to verify: git push of branches and worktrees, chezmoi templates and password-manager integration, restic/borg encryption and Backblaze B2 support, Nix/devcontainer rebuilds, and where Claude Code keeps its settings, skills, MCP configs, hooks and transcripts (~/.claude, project .claude, .mcp.json). The section recommends a layered baseline: push everything to git remotes, keep dotfiles and agent config in chezmoi, rebuild tools from a declarative bootstrap script, take encrypted restic snapshots of state that cannot be rebuilt, and keep secrets only in a password manager, never in a backup. It then gives a checklist of what to back up, a numbered restore procedure for a new machine with a target time of a few hours and a quarterly drill, and a list of trade-offs and limitations, with a citation for every tool behavior it claims. It leaves out cloud workstation providers and cost analysis.

children.title: Cloud workstations for agent workloads
children.task: Research hosted development environments that let one person keep long-running AI coding agents working while their laptop is off, lost or replaced. Compare options such as GitHub Codespaces, Gitpod/Ona, Coder, DevPod, cloud VMs (AWS/GCP/Azure/Hetzner) reached over SSH with tmux or mosh, Tailscale-based remote access, and vendor-run cloud agent sessions such as Claude Code on the web or cloud sessions. Compare them on persistence across disconnects, how long agents can run unattended, how they connect to editors and phones, GPU/CPU/RAM limits, how secrets are injected, the security of running agents with broad permissions on them (isolation, network egress, blast radius), and lock-in. State only each option's pricing model; detailed cost modeling belongs to another section. Leave out backup of the local machine and how multiple agents are orchestrated. Deliverable: a brief section (about 800-1200 words) with a comparison table, a recommended default architecture for a solo developer, and the main risks and limitations, citing current sources and dating any facts that change over time.
children.rationale: This node covers about ten products on eight dimensions, and every fact needs a current, dated source. That is too much checking for one sitting. The options fall into three groups that can be researched separately with the same columns, so the parent can merge the rows into one table and write the recommended architecture.

children.title: Managed cloud development environment platforms
children.task: Context: this is part of a research brief on how one person can run reliable, long-running AI coding agents (such as Claude Code) on hosted machines that keep working while their laptop is off, lost or replaced. Research these managed or self-hostable cloud development environment platforms: GitHub Codespaces, Ona (formerly Gitpod), Coder (OSS and Premium), and DevPod (Loft Labs). Also check whether DevPod is still actively maintained. Compare each one on the same eight columns: (1) persistence across disconnects and idle or auto-stop behavior, including timeouts and retention limits; (2) how long an agent can run unattended before the platform stops it; (3) how it connects to editors (VS Code, JetBrains, SSH) and to phones or browsers; (4) CPU, RAM and GPU limits or available machine sizes; (5) how secrets are injected; (6) security when an agent runs with broad permissions: isolation, network egress controls, blast radius; (7) lock-in and portability, for example devcontainer.json support or self-hosting; (8) pricing model only (per-hour, per-seat, free tier, self-hosted), with no cost modeling. Leave out backing up the local machine and how multiple agents are orchestrated. Cite current primary sources such as official docs, pricing pages and changelogs, and put an as-of date on every fact that changes over time. Deliverable: a markdown comparison table with one row per platform and the eight columns, then 150-300 words on the main risks and limitations of this category for running agents unattended, then one short paragraph on when this category is the right default for a solo developer.
children.rationale: This node can't be split further, and the scope is already tight: four named platforms compared on eight fixed columns.
children.result: The work means reading current primary sources for GitHub Codespaces, Ona (formerly Gitpod), Coder OSS/Premium and DevPod: official docs, pricing pages, changelogs and DevPod's GitHub release and commit activity. Each eight-column fact gets an "as of 2026-10" date, and DevPod's maintenance status gets a verdict backed by evidence. The output is a markdown table with one row per platform covering persistence and idle timeouts, unattended run limits, editor and phone or browser access, machine sizes and GPU, secrets injection, isolation and egress controls, portability through devcontainer.json or self-hosting, and pricing model, with source links. After the table come 150-300 words on the risks of running agents unattended in this category (idle auto-stop killing long jobs, retention-driven deletion, broad-permission blast radius, weak egress controls, vendor and pricing changes), then one short paragraph on when this is the right default for a solo developer.

children.title: Self-managed cloud VMs with remote access
children.task: Context: this is part of a research brief on how one person can run reliable, long-running AI coding agents (such as Claude Code) on hosted machines that keep working while their laptop is off, lost or replaced. Research a self-managed VM that the developer runs in the cloud, on AWS EC2 / Lightsail, GCP Compute Engine, Azure VMs or Hetzner Cloud, together with the remote-access stack around it: SSH with tmux or mosh for sessions that survive disconnects, Tailscale (including Tailscale SSH, ACLs and exit nodes) for private access with no public ports, and editor or phone access through VS Code Remote-SSH, JetBrains Gateway and mobile SSH or mosh clients such as Blink or Termius. Treat the providers as rows, plus one row for the Tailscale + tmux/mosh access layer. Compare them on the same eight columns: (1) persistence across disconnects; (2) how long an agent can run unattended, including spot or preemptible interruptions and maintenance events; (3) how it connects to editors and phones; (4) CPU, RAM and GPU options and quota limits; (5) how secrets are injected, for example cloud secret managers, instance metadata roles, or env files; (6) security when an agent runs with broad permissions: VM isolation, firewall and egress control, cloud IAM blast radius, and snapshots for recovery; (7) lock-in and portability; (8) pricing model only (per-hour, monthly cap, egress billing), with no cost modeling. Leave out backing up the local laptop and how multiple agents are orchestrated. Cite current primary sources and put an as-of date on every fact that changes over time. Deliverable: a markdown comparison table with the eight columns, then 150-300 words on the main risks and limitations, including the patching and ops work the developer has to carry, then one short paragraph on when this category is the right default for a solo developer.
children.rationale: This node cannot be split further, and the scope is already narrow: five rows (EC2/Lightsail, GCP Compute Engine, Azure VMs, Hetzner Cloud, plus the Tailscale + tmux/mosh access layer) compared on eight fixed columns, which one agent can research directly.
children.result: The work starts by pulling current primary sources: provider docs and pricing pages for EC2/Lightsail, Compute Engine, Azure VMs and Hetzner Cloud, covering spot/preemptible interruption notices, maintenance and live-migration policy, quotas, secret managers, metadata roles, IAM and egress billing. It also covers the docs for Tailscale (SSH, ACLs, exit nodes), tmux, mosh, VS Code Remote-SSH, JetBrains Gateway, Blink and Termius. Each fact that changes over time gets an as-of date (2026-10-28) and a link. The output is a markdown table with five rows (the four providers plus one row for the Tailscale + tmux/mosh access layer) on the eight required columns. Pricing is limited to the billing model, with no cost estimates. After the table come 150-300 words on the main risks and limitations: OS and package patching, agent credentials that can reach too much of the cloud account (IAM blast radius), egress control, snapshot discipline, spot evictions and single-VM failure. The brief ends with one short paragraph on when a self-managed VM is the right default for a solo developer.

children.title: Vendor-run cloud agent sessions
children.task: Context: this is part of a research brief on how one person can run reliable, long-running AI coding agents on hosted infrastructure that keeps working while their laptop is off, lost or replaced. Research vendor-run cloud agent sessions, where the AI vendor hosts the sandbox: Claude Code on the web and Claude Code cloud sessions (including starting or moving sessions to the cloud and steering them from the mobile app), plus the closest comparable services: OpenAI Codex cloud tasks, the GitHub Copilot coding agent, and Cursor background or cloud agents. Compare them on the same eight columns: (1) persistence across disconnects and whether a session continues with no client attached; (2) how long a task can run unattended (time or turn limits); (3) how it connects to editors, the CLI, web and phones, and how results come back, for example as branches or pull requests; (4) the compute environment and its limits, including any GPU access, and how much setup of the environment is allowed; (5) how secrets and environment variables are injected; (6) security: sandbox isolation, network egress policy and allowlists, repository and credential scope, blast radius; (7) lock-in, both to the vendor's model and to its git host; (8) pricing model only (included in a subscription, usage-based, per task), with no cost modeling. Leave out backing up the local machine and how multiple agents are orchestrated. These products change fast: cite current official docs and announcements, and put an as-of date on every fact. Deliverable: a markdown comparison table with one row per service and the eight columns, then 150-300 words on the main risks and limitations, such as opaque environments, egress limits and dependence on a vendor, then one short paragraph on when this category is the right default for a solo developer and how it could pair with a self-managed or CDE workstation.
children.rationale: This is one comparison of five products on eight fixed columns, built from official sources. One agent can do it, and splitting is not available at depth 2 anyway.
children.result: Doing this means reading current official docs, changelogs and announcements, dated as of late October 2026, for five services: Claude Code on the web and cloud sessions (moving a session to the cloud, steering it from the mobile app), OpenAI Codex cloud tasks, the GitHub Copilot coding agent, and Cursor background or cloud agents. For each one I pull the facts for the eight columns: persistence when no client is attached, run-time or turn limits, ways to connect and how results come back (branches or PRs), compute limits and GPU access, how secrets are injected, sandbox and egress policy, model and git-host lock-in, and the pricing model. Every fact gets a cited URL and an as-of date. The output is one markdown table with one row per service. After it come 150-300 words on the risks: an opaque base image, egress allowlists that break installs, short-lived sandboxes, credential scope, and dependence on a single vendor and on GitHub. A short closing paragraph says when vendor-hosted sessions are the right default for a solo developer, and how to pair them with a self-managed VM or CDE for long-running, GPU or custom-network work.

children.title: Multi-agent coordination patterns
children.task: Research how one person can run many AI coding agents at once (from a few up to dozens, including hierarchical orchestrator-to-worker trees several levels deep) without the agents colliding or losing work. Cover: dividing tasks and choosing when to decompose and when to solve directly; isolating parallel work with git worktrees, branches or containers; where coordination state lives (task queues, issue trackers, files in the repo, shared databases) so a run can resume after a crash or machine loss; merging and resolving conflicts; human checkpoints and permission boundaries; monitoring, logging and detecting stuck or looping agents; and verification such as tests, CI gates and review agents. Survey current tooling, for example Claude Code subagents and workflows, the Claude Agent SDK, and other orchestrators and open-source frameworks, and note documented failure modes. Leave out hosting choices, personal backup and dollar budgeting. Deliverable: a brief section (about 800-1200 words) with a recommended coordination architecture, a short catalog of patterns and anti-patterns, and open problems, citing sources.
children.rationale: The node asks for seven distinct pattern areas plus a cited survey of current tooling and failure modes. That is too much research for one sitting at good quality. It falls into three parts that don't overlap: structure and state, control and verification, and the tool landscape. The parent can merge them into the recommended architecture and the pattern catalog.

children.title: Decomposition, isolation and durable coordination state
children.task: Context: this is part of a research brief on how one person can run many AI coding agents at once, from a few up to dozens, including orchestrator-to-worker trees several levels deep, without the agents colliding or losing work. Research and write about four things. (1) How to divide work, and the rules or heuristics for when an agent should decompose a task versus solve it directly, including limits on depth and fan-out. (2) How to isolate parallel work with git worktrees, per-agent branches and containers or sandboxes, with the trade-offs of each. (3) Where coordination state should live so a run can resume after a crash or the loss of a machine: task queues, issue trackers, plan or status files committed to the repo, shared databases, and the journals or checkpoints of workflow engines. (4) How work is merged back: merge order, rebasing, how conflicts are detected and resolved, and how to keep tasks small enough that they rarely conflict. Keep it tool-agnostic and name specific tools only as examples. Leave out hosting choices, personal backup, dollar budgets, monitoring, human approval and verification, which other subtasks cover. Deliverable: a section of about 400-500 words that gives a recommended approach for each of the four areas, plus 3-5 patterns and 3-5 anti-patterns, each with a one-line rationale. Cite sources inline with URLs: official docs, engineering blogs, papers.
children.rationale: The deliverable is a single 400-500 word section. Its four areas (decomposition, isolation, durable state, merge-back) are closely linked and draw on overlapping sources. Splitting it would produce fragments of about 120 words each, and a parent would still have to stitch and dedupe them, so it would add overhead without adding depth.
children.result: The work is a focused web search over primary sources. These include Anthropic's multi-agent research system post and the Claude Code subagent/worktree docs, git-worktree documentation, container/sandbox docs (devcontainers, Docker), and durable-execution docs (Temporal, LangGraph checkpointers). It also covers papers on hierarchical agent decomposition and limits on depth and fan-out. From these I would write a tool-agnostic section of about 400-500 words with one recommended approach for each of the four areas. The four areas are: when to decompose and how to cap depth and fan-out; worktrees vs branches vs containers and their trade-offs; coordination state kept in durable, machine-independent stores such as a git-committed plan/status file, an issue tracker, or a workflow-engine journal; and merge order, rebase-before-merge, conflict detection, and keeping tasks small. The section ends with 3-5 patterns and 3-5 anti-patterns, each with a one-line rationale, and cites URLs inline. Hosting, personal backup, budgets, monitoring and human approval are left out.

children.title: Human checkpoints, monitoring and verification gates
children.task: Context: this is part of a research brief on how one person can run many AI coding agents at once, from a few up to dozens, including orchestrator-to-worker trees several levels deep, without the agents colliding or losing work. Research and write about three things. (1) Human checkpoints and permission boundaries: which actions need approval (push, merge, deploy, deleting data, network access), how to scope permissions per agent or per level of the tree with allowlists, sandbox modes and read-only roles, and how to batch approvals so one person is not flooded. (2) Monitoring and logging: structured logs and traces across a tree of agents, dashboards, and how to detect agents that are stuck, looping, thrashing or drifting from their task, using signals such as repeated tool calls, no progress on diffs, token or turn budgets and timeouts, and what to do on detection (kill, retry, escalate). (3) Verification: tests and CI gates that must pass before a merge, review agents and how independent they should be from the author agent, LLM-as-judge limits, and checks that catch an agent claiming success falsely. Keep it tool-agnostic and name specific tools only as examples. Leave out hosting choices, personal backup, dollar budgets, task decomposition, isolation and merge mechanics, which other subtasks cover. Deliverable: a section of about 400-500 words that gives a recommended approach for each of the three areas, plus 3-5 patterns and 3-5 anti-patterns, each with a one-line rationale. Cite sources inline with URLs.
children.rationale: One agent can cover all three areas (checkpoints, monitoring, verification) in a single 400-500 word section, and they cross-reference each other heavily. Splitting would produce three ~150-word fragments plus merge overhead for no gain in depth.
children.result: The work is a short web research pass followed by writing one section. The research covers: agent permission and sandbox models, such as Claude Code permission modes and allowlists, Codex sandbox and approval policies, and devcontainer or read-only roles; approval batching and protected branches; tracing for agent trees, such as OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, Langfuse or LangSmith traces, and step and turn limits in agent SDKs; stuck and loop detection signals; and verification, including required CI status checks, independent reviewer agents, LLM-as-judge bias studies, and reports of agents faking passing tests. The output is a tool-agnostic section of about 400-500 words. It gives one recommended approach each for (1) human checkpoints and per-level permission scoping with batched approvals, (2) structured tracing across the tree with stuck, loop and drift detection and a kill, retry or escalate policy, and (3) verification gates that rely on CI and independent review over the author's claims. It ends with 3-5 patterns and 3-5 anti-patterns, each with a one-line rationale and inline source URLs. It leaves out hosting, backup, cost, decomposition and merge mechanics.

children.title: Orchestration tooling survey and documented failure modes
children.task: Context: this is part of a research brief on how one person can run many AI coding agents at once, from a few up to dozens, including hierarchical orchestrator-to-worker trees. Survey the current tooling as of late 2026: Claude Code subagents, Agent Teams and workflow or orchestration features, the Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Codex and the Agents SDK, and open-source orchestrators and frameworks such as LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen/AG2 and OpenHands, plus parallel-agent runners built on git worktrees and any other notable ones. For each tool give: what kind of topology it supports (flat, fan-out, nested hierarchy), how it persists or resumes state, whether it isolates parallel work, and its notable limits. Then collect documented failure modes of multi-agent coding systems from papers, for example taxonomies of multi-agent LLM failures, and from vendor engineering posts or postmortems. Examples: context loss at handoffs, duplicated or conflicting work, runaway fan-out, false completion claims, and orchestrators that fail to verify their workers. List the open problems that remain. Verify claims against primary sources; where a feature's status is uncertain, say so. Leave out hosting choices, personal backup and dollar budgets. Deliverable: a compact comparison table of 6-10 tools, a list of 5-8 documented failure modes, each with a source, and 3-5 open problems. Keep the prose to about 400-500 words, cite sources inline with URLs, and date-stamp the survey.
children.rationale: This node is at its split limit, and the task is a single survey that one agent can finish: check each tool's docs and the main failure papers, then fill one table and two short lists.
children.result: The first step is to check primary sources directly with WebSearch and WebFetch, as of 2026-10-28. The sources are Anthropic docs for Claude Code subagents, Agent Teams, workflows and the Agent SDK, OpenAI docs for Codex and the Agents SDK, and the repos and docs for LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen/AG2, OpenHands, and worktree-based runners such as Claude Squad, Conductor and container-use. For each tool I record four things: topology (flat, fan-out or nested), how it persists or resumes state, whether it isolates parallel work, and its notable limits. I mark any feature as uncertain when it is experimental, renamed or undocumented. Next, I collect 5-8 failure modes with sources: the MAST taxonomy paper "Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" (arXiv 2503.13657), Anthropic's multi-agent research-system engineering post, Cognition's "Don't Build Multi-Agents", and relevant SWE-bench or postmortem write-ups. The modes include context loss at handoffs, duplicated or conflicting edits, runaway fan-out, false completion claims and missing verification by the orchestrator. The output is a dated 400-500-word section: a 6-10-row comparison table, a sourced list of failure modes, and 3-5 open problems, with URLs cited inline and no material on hosting, backup or cost.

children.title: Cost control for agents and infrastructure
children.task: Research how a solo developer keeps the money spent on a multi-agent coding setup predictable and bounded. Cover: LLM spending (subscription plans compared with pay-as-you-go API pricing, per-model price differences, prompt caching, batch APIs, choosing models by task tier, context-size discipline, token usage tracking and usage limits); cloud compute spending (auto-stop and idle shutdown, spot or preemptible instances, storage and egress charges, budgets and billing alerts on major clouds); guardrails against runaway agents (per-run token or dollar caps, rate limits, kill switches, alerting); and a worked example monthly budget at light, moderate and heavy usage, with all assumptions stated. Check current prices against official pricing pages and give the date checked; mark estimates as estimates. Leave out how backups work, comparisons of workstation features, and orchestration design except where they directly drive cost. Deliverable: a brief section (about 800-1200 words) with a cost model table, a guardrail checklist, and limitations of the estimates, citing sources.
children.rationale: The deliverable is one section of 800-1200 words, and the worked budget needs the LLM and cloud prices in a single model. Splitting it would produce fragments of about 500 words each and a merge step that has to reconcile two sets of assumptions.
children.result: Doing this means checking current prices on the official pages. On the LLM side: Anthropic's API pricing and Claude Pro/Max plans, plus OpenAI's and Google's API pricing for per-model tiers, prompt caching and batch discounts. On the cloud side: one or two on-demand and spot VM rates, plus disk and egress rates, from AWS, GCP and Azure. It also means reading the docs on usage limits and alerts: Anthropic Console spend limits, Claude Code usage reporting, AWS Budgets, GCP budget alerts and Azure Cost Management, along with the auto-stop features. The output is a cited section of about 1000 words with the check date (2026-10-28) on every price. It contains a cost model table for light, moderate and heavy months that states each assumption (sessions per day, tokens per session, cache hit rate, model mix, VM hours, storage), labels the estimates, and compares a subscription with pay-as-you-go. It also has a guardrail checklist (per-run token or dollar caps, rate limits, kill switches, idle shutdown, billing alerts) and a limitations paragraph covering price volatility, opaque subscription limits, variance in token use, and regional and currency differences.
